name: Motivated forgetting
statement: Deliberately keeping a memory out of awareness when a reminder appears is claimed to make that memory harder to recall later.
meaning: Motivated forgetting is the umbrella term for forgetting produced by active processes rather than by time or interference. Anderson and Hanslmayr define it as increased forgetting arising from active processes that down-prioritise unwanted experiences in service of creating or sustaining an emotional or cognitive state. Two laboratory paradigms carry most of the weight, and they are different tasks. Directed forgetting attaches a forget or a remember instruction to material as it is studied, either item by item or to a whole list, so it acts on encoding. The think/no-think task trains cue and target to criterion first, then presents the cue and asks the person to keep the target out of mind. Only the second models the situation the clinical literature cares about, where a reminder arrives and the memory is unwelcome. The measure is recall of suppressed items against baseline items that were studied and then left alone. Testing with a cue that never appeared in the experiment, called an independent probe, is what separates damage to the memory itself from interference at the trained cue.

origin.who: Michael C. Anderson and Collin Green
origin.note: Anderson and Green's think/no-think experiments are what the current literature is built on, and their paper names Freud's repression as the hypothesis under test. The label is older. Glucksberg and King published a laboratory analogue of repression in Science in 1967 under the heading of motivated forgetting, Weiner and Higgins called that paradigm confounded in 1969, and Glucksberg and Ornstein replied in the same issue. Those three are described here from their titles and Crossref records and were not read. Anderson and Hanslmayr's 2014 review is the paper that gathers directed forgetting and retrieval suppression under the one term.

evidence: Anderson and Green ran four experiments. Thirty-two students took part in each of the first three and sixteen in the fourth. Each learned 40 critical word pairs and 10 filler pairs, drilled until at least half the pairs were recalled correctly. The think/no-think phase gave 377 trials, with each cue on screen for up to 4 s. Five pairs sat in each of the 0, 1, 8 and 16 repetition conditions for both the respond and the suppress instruction, and the 0 condition was the baseline. A suppression cue had to be fixated for the full four seconds, and saying the target set off an error beep. Recall of suppressed items fell below baseline, and the drop grew with the number of suppression attempts, while recall of respond items rose. The paper reports the inhibition effect between 0 and 16 suppressions as significant at P < 0.01 in every experiment, and at P < 0.05 in every same-probe and independent-probe test in experiments 1 to 3. The independent probe supplied a category name and a first letter, insect r for the target roach, so the impairment could not be put down to interference at the trained cue. Experiment 2 paid 25 cents per correct answer up to $4 and the pattern held. Experiment 3 told participants that the researchers expected suppression to improve memory, a story they believed at a mean rating of 4.2 on a five-point scale, and the pattern held again. Experiment 4 dropped the instruction to control awareness and asked only that the answer not be spoken aloud. Recall did not decline with repetitions, F < 1 in all cases, and inhibition was reliably larger in experiments 1 to 3 than in experiment 4, P < 0.05. Condition means are plotted in the paper's figures and not printed, so no recall percentage from the original is quoted here. Liu, Hulbert, Yang, Guo, Qiu and Anderson later tested 497 participants and found the forgetting. Their abstract reports its magnitude as negatively correlated with participants' reported compliance on no-think trials, on both probe types, and their conclusion is that failure to follow the no-think instruction compromises the effect. Test expectancy was not associated with it. The directed-forgetting literature is larger and steadier. Hall, Fawcett, Hourihan and Fawcett's meta-analysis of the item method found remember items recalled better than forget items by 19.6%, 95% CI [16.1, 23.1], for neutral material and by 15.1%, CI [12.4, 17.7], for emotional material, a within-study gap of 4.2%, CI [2.0, 6.4]. Pevie, Baldwin, Fawcett, Lahey and Fawcett screened 823 articles, kept 36, and found directed forgetting reduced in clinical groups, which is the same direction the think/no-think meta-analysis reports for anxiety and depression.

replication.headline: A meta-analysis of 96 effects from 25 studies puts suppression-induced forgetting at 0.28 in healthy people while warning that publication bias may inflate it, and a preregistered replication of 150 people found d = 0.03.
replication.detail: Bulevich, Roediger, Balota and Butler ran three experiments modelled on Anderson and Green, with the same 1, 8 and 16 repetitions and the same two probe types. None showed reliable suppression on either probe, and they concluded that suppression is not a robust phenomenon in the paradigm. Wessel, Albers, Zandstra and Heininga published two replications from the 2000s that had sat unpublished, N = 49 and N = 36, alongside a reanalysis of two published studies, and ran every defensible analysis in parallel. Same-probe results were mixed and independent-probe tests were mostly non-significant, which they treat as a problem for the inhibition account. Wiechert and six colleagues ran a preregistered online version with an experimenter present on a video call, testing 150 English-speaking adults, 89 of them female, mean age 31.14. Neither probe gave the effect: same probe BF01 = 7.84, d = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.13, 0.20]; independent probe BF01 = 5.71, d = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.12, 0.24]. Wessel, Lehmann and Wiechert then adapted that procedure for undergraduates. A first study of 54 students in the laboratory found the effect. A second ran 54 in the laboratory and 54 online, and found it in the laboratory and not online. Their exploratory Bayesian analyses gave conclusive evidence for a null in the online arm without establishing that the two settings differed. On the other side, Liu and colleagues found the effect in 497 participants. Stramaccia, Meyer, Rischer, Fawcett and Benoit's meta-analysis of 96 effects from 25 studies gives 0.28, 95% CI [0.14, 0.43], for healthy participants, and cautions that publication bias may inflate that estimate. The same meta-analysis reports -0.21, CI [-0.41, -0.02], for more anxious people, 0.05, CI [-0.19, 0.29], for depressed people, and 0.42, CI [0.32, 0.52], for people with a repressive coping style. The dispute has an answer scheduled. Fawcett, Levy, Bergström, Bulevich, Clark, Hertel, Hulbert, MacLeod, Todorovic, van Schie and the Memory Control Consortium hold an in-principle acceptance at Nature Human Behaviour for a multisite replication. The registered sample is 3,984 participants across 78 contributing groups, half under thought-avoidance and half under thought-substitution instructions, with collection running to 1 April 2024. Their protocol deliberately does not copy the 2001 procedure, on the grounds that the task has changed since, and it powers the design to detect d of about 0.15. Searches of Crossref, PubMed and Europe PMC in August 2026 returned no Stage 2 report.

limits: This entry covers the think/no-think paradigm and, for contrast, item-method directed forgetting. It does not cover retrieval-induced forgetting, the neuroimaging work, Wegner's thought suppression, or children's memory. The search ran across Crossref, DataCite, PubMed, Europe PMC and the open web. Taylor and Francis returned 403 for the full texts of Wessel and colleagues' multiverse paper and of Wiechert and colleagues' replication, so both were read in abstract, the multiverse paper also through its fourth author's summary page. Stramaccia and colleagues' meta-analysis was read in abstract, and that abstract gives 0.28 without naming a metric. The multisite protocol, read in full, describes the same figure as d = 0.28 and gives d = 0.66 and 0.59 for the thought-avoidance and thought-substitution instructions. Those two figures are quoted at one remove and are kept out of the structured fields. Anderson and Green plot their condition means rather than printing them, which is why no recall percentage from the original appears above. Liu and colleagues' paper was read in abstract, and the abstract states the compliance correlation as negative while the conclusion runs the other way, so the direction of coding is not settled here. The paradigm uses neutral word pairs learned and tested in one session, and the whole of experiment 1's suppression effort came to about a minute per item. Wessel's review of independent-probe suppression concludes that no reliable overall effect size is available for it, that the extent of publication and reporting bias is unknown, and that autobiographical memories are hard to study this way.
misreadings: Motivated forgetting and directed forgetting get treated as one result. Directed forgetting attaches its instruction to material as it is studied and acts on encoding. The think/no-think task trains the pair to criterion and then attacks retrieval when the cue returns. Anderson and Green drew the line themselves, writing that directed forgetting shows a controllable inhibition process limited in scope to an immediately preceding temporal interval. The evidence behind the two is unequal. Item-method directed forgetting is a 19.6% recall difference in a meta-analysis of neutral material; suppression-induced forgetting is 0.28 with publication bias unresolved. A failed think/no-think study is then read as proof that nobody can forget on purpose. Liu and colleagues' compliance result points at a duller explanation, which is that the no-think instruction often goes unfollowed. Anderson and Green's paper is quoted as showing Freud was right. It offers itself as a model of repression, and Wessel's review of the independent-probe evidence concludes that it is a doubtful one. Whether trauma can be repressed and later recovered is a separate argument and still a live one: Otgaar, Howe, Patihis, Merckelbach, Lynn, Lilienfeld and Loftus put belief in repressed memories at 58% and argue the memory wars never ended. This page records what the laboratory task has and has not shown and takes no side on that. Motivated forgetting also runs the opposite way from this atlas's entries on false memory and suggestibility, which are about acquiring a memory of something that did not happen rather than losing access to one that did.
